audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Since final exams are about four weeks away, I'd like to go over our attendance and leave rules before things get busy. First, if you're absent for more than one third of the class hours in any course, the instructor can refuse to let you take the final exam. That rule is strict, so keep track of your own absences on the student portal.

Second, there are different types of leave. Sick leave and family emergency leave can be requested after you return, but personal leave must be requested before the class. Personal leave is limited to six class hours per course each semester.

Finally, approved leave does not cancel your assignments. You still need to contact your instructor and agree on a new deadline. If you're facing a long-term problem, such as a serious illness, come see me early. We can talk about options like reducing your course load instead of failing a class.

head: From: Dr. Amy Hsu <amyhsu@university.edu.tw>
To: Students in Introduction to Sociology
Subject: Extension Requests for the Final Project
passage: Several of you have asked about extensions for the final project, which is due on December 18. To keep things fair, I will only consider requests that are submitted through the course website at least five days before the deadline. Please explain your reason briefly and suggest a realistic new date.

Extensions will generally be granted for illness, family emergencies, or schedule conflicts with official university events. Heavy workloads in other courses are understandable, but they are not, by themselves, a valid reason. Requests made after the deadline will not be accepted unless there is a documented emergency.
If your request is approved, you will receive a confirmation email within two working days. Please keep this email, as it serves as your record.

passage: When the Office of Academic Affairs moved all leave requests online two years ago, many students welcomed the change. Instead of chasing signatures from their advisor, department office, and instructor, they could now fill out a single form on their phones. According to the office, the average processing time dropped from five days to less than two. Students who are sick or dealing with a family emergency can even submit a request after they return, as long as they upload supporting documents within a week.

However, a recent survey by the Student Association suggests that the system is not working equally well for everyone. Of the 1,200 students who responded, about 70 percent said the online process was faster. Yet nearly a quarter complained that instructors often approved requests without giving any guidance on missed work. "My leave was approved in an hour, but I still had no idea how to make up the lab," said one third-year chemistry student.

Some faculty members admit the problem. Professor Wu Ming-hui of the History Department says the system makes approval "almost too easy." "In the past, a student had to talk to me in person, so we naturally discussed what they had missed. Now I just click a button," she explained. She now sends a short message to every student whose leave she approves, asking them to visit her office hours within a week.

The Student Association has proposed two improvements: adding a required section where instructors list makeup arrangements, and sending automatic reminders before makeup deadlines. The Office of Academic Affairs says it will test both features in selected departments next semester before deciding whether to use them campus-wide. Until then, students are encouraged to contact their instructors directly as soon as their leave is approved.

questions.explain: 全文先說線上系統加快速度，再指出老師核准後缺乏補課指引的溝通落差，故選 B。A 與 70% 認為較快相反；D 學生會只提出改善建議，並非取代。
options: Students prefer paper forms to online leave requests.

Professors want to stop approving leave requests.
